subject: physics

items.q: In which of these situations is work done on the object by the force described?
items.correct: A sledge is pulled forwards and slides 4 m along the ground
items.misconception: A shopper stands still holding a heavy bag for a minute
items.why: In everyday English 'work' means effort, and holding a heavy object is tiring, so students judge work by how hard it feels rather than by whether the object moves. In physics, work is done only when a force causes a displacement. With no movement, s = 0, so W = F × 0 = 0 J of work is done on the bag no matter how tiring holding it is.
items.random_wrong: A waiter walks 5 m holding a loaded tray level in one hand

items.q: A student holds a box weighing 40 N at a constant height for 15 s. How much work does the student's upward force do on the box?
items.why: Everyday language ties work to time spent, and time appears in the closely related idea of power, so students smuggle time into W = F s. Time does not appear in W = F s. Work done depends only on the force and the distance moved along its line of action; how quickly the work is done is power, a different quantity.

items.q: A cyclist pushes a broken bike with a steady force of 25 N along the line of action of the force, moving it 80 m. What is the work done on the bike?
items.why: Students meet several equations of the form quantity = quantity ÷ quantity (speed, density, pressure) and apply that pattern to W = F s without checking it. W = F s means work done = force multiplied by distance. Dividing gives neither joules nor a sensible size; multiply the force by the distance moved along its line of action.

items.q: Which symbol equation matches 'work done = force × distance (moved along the line of action of the force)'?
items.why: Students meet several equations of the form quantity = quantity ÷ quantity (speed, density, pressure) and apply that pattern to W = F s without checking it. W = F s means work done = force multiplied by distance. Dividing gives neither joules nor a sensible size; multiply the force by the distance moved along its line of action.

items.q: In the equation W = F s, which units belong with each quantity?
items.correct: W in joules, F in newtons, s in metres
items.misconception: W in newtons, F in joules, s in metres
items.why: Students read compound units as belonging to the first unit named, and newtons are strongly linked to force from the start of the forces topic. A newton-metre comes from multiplying a force in newtons by a distance in metres, which is work done. It equals one joule; force is measured in newtons alone.
items.random_wrong: W in joules, F in newtons, s in centimetres

items.q: One joule of work is done in which of these situations?
items.correct: A force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre
items.misconception: A force of one newton acts on an object for one second
items.why: Everyday language ties work to time spent, and time appears in the closely related idea of power, so students smuggle time into W = F s. Time does not appear in W = F s. Work done depends only on the force and the distance moved along its line of action; how quickly the work is done is power, a different quantity.
items.random_wrong: A force of one newton moves an object 1 m sideways

items.q: A machine does 4500 N m of work. What is this work done in joules?
items.why: Almost every other conversion students meet (mm to m, g to kg, kJ to J) involves a factor of 10, 100 or 1000, so they expect a factor here too. The newton-metre and the joule are the same unit under two names: 1 joule = 1 newton-metre. Converting changes the words only, so 4500 N m = 4500 J.

items.q: Which statement about newton-metres and joules is correct?
items.correct: 1 newton-metre of work is exactly equal to 1 joule of work
items.misconception: 1 newton-metre of work is equal to 1000 joules of work
items.why: Almost every other conversion students meet (mm to m, g to kg, kJ to J) involves a factor of 10, 100 or 1000, so they expect a factor here too. The newton-metre and the joule are the same unit under two names: 1 joule = 1 newton-metre. Converting changes the words only, so 4500 N m = 4500 J.
items.random_wrong: The newton-metre measures force, the joule measures work

items.q: A student lifts a box steadily from the floor onto a shelf. Which best describes the energy transfer as work is done on the box?
items.correct: Chemical store of the student to gravitational potential store of the box
items.misconception: Chemical store of the student to the kinetic store of the box as it rises
items.why: The first example of work most students meet is a force accelerating an object, so they attach work permanently to movement getting faster. Work done transfers energy, but not always to the kinetic store. Lifting at a steady speed fills the gravitational potential store; dragging against friction fills thermal stores.
items.random_wrong: Gravitational potential store of the box to chemical store of the student

items.q: A car brakes and comes to rest. Work is done against the frictional forces at the brakes. Which best describes what happens?
items.correct: The kinetic store of the car empties and the brakes rise in temperature
items.misconception: The kinetic store of the car empties and the energy is destroyed
items.why: Teachers and textbooks say energy is 'lost to friction', and the warming is too small to feel, so students conclude the energy has gone rather than moved. Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object. The energy is transferred to thermal stores, not destroyed.
items.random_wrong: The kinetic store empties and the brakes stay at the same temperature

items.q: What is the effect of work being done against the frictional forces acting on an object?
items.correct: The temperature of the object rises
items.misconception: The energy of the object is destroyed
items.why: Teachers and textbooks say energy is 'lost to friction', and the warming is too small to feel, so students conclude the energy has gone rather than moved. Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object. The energy is transferred to thermal stores, not destroyed.
items.random_wrong: The object slows but does not warm

items.q: A cyclist brakes for a long time going downhill and the brake blocks become hot. Why?
items.correct: Work is done against friction, so the blocks rise in temperature
items.misconception: Friction destroys the bike's energy and heat is what is left over
items.why: Teachers and textbooks say energy is 'lost to friction', and the warming is too small to feel, so students conclude the energy has gone rather than moved. Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object. The energy is transferred to thermal stores, not destroyed.
items.random_wrong: The blocks gain energy in their kinetic store and so become hot

items.q: A porter carries a 60 N suitcase 20 m along a level corridor, keeping it at a constant height. How much work does the upward supporting force do on the suitcase?
items.why: Students learn W = F s as 'force times distance' and substitute whatever distance the question gives, without checking the direction that distance was travelled in. The equation is work done = force × distance moved along the line of action of the force. Horizontal movement is at right angles to the upward force, so that distance is zero and the upward force does no work.

items.q: A box is dragged 5 m by a steady 30 N force. It is then dragged 10 m by the same 30 N force. How does the work done compare?
items.correct: It doubles, because work done is force × distance and the distance doubles
items.misconception: It stays the same, because the same size of force is used on both journeys
items.why: Everyday language ties work to time spent, and time appears in the closely related idea of power, so students smuggle time into W = F s. Time does not appear in W = F s. Work done depends only on the force and the distance moved along its line of action; how quickly the work is done is power, a different quantity.
items.random_wrong: It quadruples, because the force and the distance have both been doubled

items.q: A force of 12 N pushes a book 50 cm across a desk along the line of action of the force. What is the work done on the book?
items.why: Students substitute the numbers as printed and only check units at the end, if at all, so a distance in centimetres slips through unconverted. In W = F s the distance, s, is in metres. Convert first: 50 cm = 0.50 m, giving W = 12 × 0.50 = 6 J.

items.q: A cleaner pushes a trolley at a steady speed across a rough floor with a force of 25 N for 8 m, doing 200 J of work. What happens to that 200 J?
items.correct: It is transferred to thermal stores, so the trolley rises in temperature
items.misconception: It is transferred to the kinetic store, so the trolley gets faster and faster
items.why: The first example of work most students meet is a force accelerating an object, so they attach work permanently to movement getting faster. Work done transfers energy, but not always to the kinetic store. Lifting at a steady speed fills the gravitational potential store; dragging against friction fills thermal stores.
items.random_wrong: It is used up in overcoming friction, so that energy no longer exists

items.q: A cyclist brakes hard for a long time on a hill. What happens to the brake blocks?
items.correct: Their temperature rises, because work is done against the frictional forces acting on them.
items.misconception: Friction just slows things down; something has to be heated by a flame or a heater before its temperature can rise.
items.why: Temperature rise is first taught alongside heating, so students file friction under 'slowing down' and never connect it to a rise in temperature. Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object. Brake blocks, drills and rubbed hands all get hotter for this reason.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which quantities are measured in joules?
items.correct: Work done and energy transferred are both measured in joules, and 1 joule = 1 newton-metre.
items.misconception: Joules are for heat and food energy; mechanical work must be measured in some other unit.
items.why: Joules are usually met first in heating and in nutrition labels, so students tie the unit to those contexts rather than to energy transfer in general. Doing work is a way of transferring energy, so work done is measured in the same unit as energy: the joule. A newton-metre of work is a joule of energy transferred.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.5.2 Work done and energy transfer
